_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 166 - The Kumulipo, Hawaiian creation chant (trans. Queen Liliuokalani 1897; Beckwith interlinear reference). Chants 1-2 (deep-sea life), chants 9-10 (La'ila'i and the first humans). Existing records kumulipo-genealogy and hawaiian-kumulipo cover the chant frame. Sensitivity: paraphrase only - a genealogical chant of the Kalanikauikeaouli line. Topics 1 creation, 7 cosmology. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Kumulipo: The First Night of Corals and Shells
title.zh: 生命源起：第一夜的珊瑚與螺貝

region.en: Hawaiian chant sung at Honaunau (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷霍瑙瑙誦唱地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 18th c. for Ka-I-i-mamao; recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897

source.work: The Kumulipo, Hawaiian creation chant, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (San Francisco 1897); interlinear ed. M. W. Beckwith (1951)

summary.en: When the earth grew hot and the heavens turned about, and the sun was darkened that the moon might shine, there was nothing but night; night gave birth to Kumulipo, a male, and Po'ele, a female. From the darkness slip into light the first born of the sea: the coral polyp, the grub that heaps the earth, starfish, sea cucumbers, sea urchins, barnacles and pearl oysters, mussels and limpets, cowries and conch - each with its child. 'Born was man for the narrow stream, the woman for the broad stream; the god enters, man cannot enter.'
summary.zh: 地熱翻滾、天穹旋轉、日暗月明之際，唯有長夜；夜生男庫穆利波與女波埃萊。黑暗滑入光明，海中初生者次第而出：珊瑚蟲、掘地之蟲、海星、海參、海膽、藤壺珍珠貝、蚌螺之屬——各攜其子。經文反覆吟詠：『男屬細流，女屬寬流；神可入，人不可入。』

sensitivity.note: Genealogical chant of Hawaiian ali'i line; paraphrase of the Liliuokalani public-domain translation only.

passages.text: At the time when the earth became hot, at the time when the heavens turned about, at the time when the sun was darkened, to cause the moon to shine, the time of the rise of the Pleiades - the slime, this was the source of the earth. The source of the darkness that made darkness; the source of the night that made night. The intense darkness, the deep darkness; darkness of the sun, darkness of the night - nothing but night. The night gave birth: born was Kumulipo in the night, a male; born was Po'ele in the night, a female.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant one (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Born was the coral polyp, born was the coral, came forth. Born was the grub that digs and heaps up the earth; born was his child, an earthworm. Born was the starfish, his child the small starfish came forth; born was the sea cucumber, his child the small sea cucumber; born was the sea urchin, and the short-spiked sea urchin, the smooth sea urchin with its child the long-spiked, the ring-shaped with its child the thin-spiked; born was the barnacle, his child the pearl oyster; born was the mother-of-pearl, his child the oyster; born was the mussel, his child the hermit crab; born was the big limpet, his child the small limpet; born was the cowry, his child the small cowry; born was the conch shell, his child the small conch shell; born was the nerita shellfish and the sand-burrowing shellfish; born was the fresh water shellfish, his child the small fresh water shellfish came forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant one (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Born was man for the narrow stream, the woman for the broad stream. Born was the Ekaha moss living in the sea, guarded by the Ekahakaha fern living on land; darkness slips into light; earth and water are the food of the plant. The god enters, man cannot enter. Born was the tough seagrass living in the sea, guarded by the tough landgrass living on land; born was the Ala'ala moss, guarded by the Ala'ala mint; born was the Manauea moss, guarded by the Manauea taro plant; born was the Ko'ele seaweed, guarded by the long-jointed sugarcane; born was the Puaki seaweed, guarded by the Akiaki rush living on land. Darkness slips into light; earth and water are the food of the plant; the god enters, man cannot enter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant one (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: The Second Night: Fish Born Swimming

region.zh: 夏威夷祭歌（象徵性定位，深海）

texts.period: Composed c. 18th c.; recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897

source.work: The Kumulipo, Hawaiian creation chant, chant two, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (San Francisco 1897); interlinear ed. M. W. Beckwith (1951)

summary.en: Born is a child to Po-wehiwehi, cradled in the arms of Po-uliuli, dweller in the land of Poho-mi-luamea - the sacred scent from the gourd stem proclaims itself, and the seven waters just float. Born is the child of the hilu fish and swims. Born is the porpoise in the sea there swimming; born is the shark and the goatfish; the eel and the crab; the octopus and the sting ray; the bonito and the albacore; mackerel, mullet - each born in the sea there swimming, while land creatures wait their pairing across the divided nights.
summary.zh: 波維希維希之子誕生，搖於波烏里烏里之懷，居於波霍米盧阿梅亞之境；葫蘆莖間聖香自陳，七水漂浮。希盧魚之子誕生而游。海中依次誕生：鼠海豚、鯊、山羊魚、鰻與蟹、章魚與魟、鰹與鮪、鯖與鯔——凡例皆『在海中游而誕』；陸上生靈則待各夜配對而生。

passages.text: Born is a child to Po-wehiwehi, cradled in the arms of Po-uliuli; a wrestler, a pusher; dweller in the land of Poho-mi-luamea. The sacred scent from the gourd stem proclaims itself; the stench breaks forth in the time of infancy; he is doubtful and stands swelling; he crooks himself and straddles. The seven waters just float; born is the child of the hilu fish and swims. The hilu fish rests with spreading tail-fin; a child of renown for Po-uliuli, a little one for Po-wehiwehi: Po-uliuli the male, Po-wehiwehi the female.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant two (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Born is the I'a, born the porpoise in the sea there swimming; born is the shark, born the goatfish, in the sea there swimming; born is the Mau and the Maumau; the Nana and the Mana; the Nake and the Make; the Napa and the Nala; the Pala and the Kala; the eel and the crab in the sea there swimming; born is the Kalakala and the Huluhulu sea slug; the Halahala and the Palapala; born is the octopus, born the sting ray in the sea there swimming; born is the Ao and the milkfish; born is the bonito, born the albacore in the sea there swimming; born is the mackerel and the Akule fish; born is the mullet and the Anae in the sea there swimming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant two (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Man for the narrow stream, woman for the broad stream - the refrain that opens each division of the chant: every sea creature born in its night has its counterpart born on land in a night to come, the pairing of sea and shore, water-thing and land-thing, running through sixteen chants until the human line of the chiefs appears. The Kumulipo sings the birth of the cosmos as a genealogy, so that the chief born at its end may claim the whole chain of life from the first darkness as his ancestors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant two and frame (Liliuokalani 1897; Beckwith 1951); not verbatim.

title.en: La'ila'i, the Woman of Nu'umealani, Mother of Men
title.zh: 神秘女子萊伊萊伊：人類之母

region.en: Nu'umealani, land of the gods (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 神居之地努烏梅阿蘭尼（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 18th c.; recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897

source.work: The Kumulipo, Hawaiian creation chant, chants nine-ten, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (San Francisco 1897); interlinear ed. M. W. Beckwith (1951)

summary.en: Still trembling stands the earth; hot, rumbling, split is the heaven - this woman ascends to heaven and the earth splits. The children of Ki'i sprung from the brain come out and fly to the heavens, marked by the ruddy tint. From the female fire-stick comes the fire that makes men; this woman dwelt in Nu'umealani, the land where the gods dwelt, stripped the dark leaves of the koa - a woman of mysterious body who lived with Ki'i, with Kane, with Kane of the time when men multiplied. She bore the Groping-one, the Dim-sighted, and last the Naked-one - part of the posterity from whom the chief's line is chanted.
summary.zh: 大地震顫而立；天穹轟裂如焚——神秘女子直上九天，大地為之坼裂。自奇伊腦髓迸出的子嗣飛昇於天，以紅暈為記。『女火棒迸出成人之火』：此女居神地努烏梅阿蘭尼，剝寇阿暗葉；身體莫測，與奇伊同居、與卡內同居、與人丁繁衍之世的卡內同居。她生下摸索者、昏昧者，最末生下赤裸者——酋長世系即自此女之後裔誦起。

sensitivity.note: The human-line opening of the Kumulipo; the female fire-stick image retained.

passages.text: Still, trembling stands earth; hot, rumbling, split is the heaven; this woman ascends to heaven, ascends right up to heaven; ascends up toward the forest. Tries to touch the earth and the earth splits up; children of Ki'i sprung from the brain came out, flew, flew also to the heavens; showed the sign, the ruddy tint by which they were known; showed the fine reddish hair at puberty; showed on the chin a reddish beard. The offspring of that mysterious woman - the woman of 'Iliponi, of within 'I'ipakalani.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant nine (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the female fire-stick comes the fire that makes men. That woman dwelt in Nu'umealani, the land where the gods dwelt; she stripped the dark leaves of the koa tree - a woman of mysterious body was this. She lived with Ki'i, she lived with Kane; she lived with Kane of the time when men multiplied; forgotten is the time of this multitude. A multitude, the posterity of the time of child-bearing; she returned again upward, dwelt in the sacred forest of the gods in Nu'umealani. Was pregnant there; the earth broke open; born was the woman Groping-one; born was Dim-sighted, a woman; last born was Naked-one, 'Olohelohe - part of the posterity of that woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant nine (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Come hither, La'ila'i to the wall: Kane of Kapokinikini to the post; Ki'i be quiet. Born was La'i-olo-olo and lived at Kapapa; born was Kamaha'ina the first-born, a male; born was Kamamule, a male; Kamakalua the second child was a girl; came the child Po'ele-i, Midnight; came the child Po'ele-a, First-light; Wehi-wela-wehi-loa, opening-to-the-heat, opening wide. La'ila'i returned and lived with Kane - so the chant moves from the mysterious ancestress to the named generations through which the Kumulipo reaches the chief for whose birth the sixteen chants were composed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant ten (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
